title: Prompt Architecture & Structured Deliberation
summary: This intermediate-level module teaches learners to decide whether reasoning should happen within one model call or across an inspectable chain of calls. After completing it, learners can structure long inputs, design acceptance checks, and verify outputs against source evidence rather than trusting narrated reasoning.
objectives: Explain what chain-of-thought prompting is, what the original research showed, and why guidance for selected reasoning models recommends clear goals instead of hand-written step-by-step instructions.
Choose between built-in model thinking, prompted reasoning, and an explicit prompt chain for a given task, justifying the choice in terms of inspectability, latency, and token cost.
Structure a long-context prompt so documents come first and the question comes last, and ground the answer in quoted evidence.
Evaluate a model's visible reasoning as unverified output rather than as a faithful record of how the answer was produced.
Build a draft, review, and revision chain in which every revision receives the original source evidence.

sections.title: Reasoning before answering, and where it now lives
paragraphs: This is an intermediate-level module. It assumes that you can write a basic prompt, distinguish instructions from source material, and recognize that a workflow may make one or more model calls. It does not require programming experience or prior knowledge of a particular provider.

Wei and colleagues named the technique that shaped much of modern prompt design in "Chain-of-Thought Prompting Elicits Reasoning in Large Language Models" (2022). A chain of thought is "a series of intermediate reasoning steps," and chain-of-thought prompting supplies a few worked examples that show those steps before the answer. The authors found that it improved the performance of sufficiently large models on arithmetic, commonsense, and symbolic reasoning tasks; prompting a 540-billion-parameter model with just eight such examples achieved state-of-the-art accuracy at the time on the GSM8K benchmark of math word problems. The mechanism fits the probabilistic picture of generation: every token a model writes becomes context for the tokens that follow, so writing intermediate steps first gives the final answer more to condition on.

Reasoning can now occur in different places. The selected provider guidance cited by this module describes model families that perform reasoning before producing an answer. Google's documentation says its Gemini 3 and 2.5 series use a "thinking process" that improves reasoning and multi-step planning. OpenAI's reasoning guide distinguishes reasoning models, described as planners for complex tasks, from lower-latency models intended for more straightforward execution. These provider-specific examples do not establish that every model reasons internally. The architectural question is which part of a particular workflow should perform the reasoning and how much latency and token use the task can afford.
sections.callout: Reasoning may occur within a model response or across separate calls. Identify the capabilities of the selected model before deciding how to word or divide the task.

sections.title: Steering a model that already thinks
paragraphs: OpenAI's reasoning best practices tell developers to keep prompts "simple and direct" and to avoid chain-of-thought prompts for its reasoning models: "Since these models perform reasoning internally, prompting them to 'think step by step' or 'explain your reasoning' is unnecessary." The same guide recommends trying zero-shot prompts before adding examples, using delimiters such as markdown, XML tags, and section titles to mark distinct parts of the input, and being "very specific about your end goal." This is guidance for the models covered by that provider document, not a rule about every model.

Reasoning also affects token use and latency. Google's documentation reports thought-token usage as part of usage information, so reasoning work must be considered when comparing workflow cost. OpenAI distinguishes reasoning models from lower-latency, more cost-efficient models intended for straightforward execution. A well-specified extraction and an ambiguous multi-document analysis may therefore deserve different model choices or reasoning depth. Compare those choices on the same evaluation cases rather than assuming that more reasoning always produces a better result.

sections.title: Chain prompts when you need to inspect the steps
paragraphs: Built-in thinking handles multistep reasoning inside one call, but it leaves you with one output to judge. Prompt chaining spreads the work across several calls instead. Google's prompting guide describes the pattern: "make each step a prompt and chain the prompts together in a sequence," so that "the output of one prompt in the sequence becomes the input of the next prompt." It lists two relatives: breaking a long list of instructions into one prompt per instruction, and aggregating the results of parallel tasks run on different portions of the data. Anthropic's guide says chaining "is still useful when you need to inspect intermediate outputs or enforce a specific pipeline structure." Its example is self-correction: generate a draft, review it against criteria, and then refine it in a separate call so each stage can be logged or evaluated.

The architectural gain is observability. Each link has its own input, output, and acceptance check, so when a final answer is wrong you can locate the step that failed instead of rewriting one large prompt and hoping. Intermediate outputs can be validated by ordinary code, routed to a person for review, or stored and reused. The costs are real: more calls add latency, shared context may have to be sent again, and an error in an early link propagates unless a check stops it. Use a chain when a step's output can be checked on its own and is worth checking. Keep work inside a single reasoning call when the steps are tightly coupled and only the end result can be judged.

A revision call must receive the evidence needed to verify its changes. Passing only the draft and review is insufficient because the reviewer may be wrong or may describe the source incompletely. In the sequence below, the original source is included in the draft, review, and revision calls.

code.label: Illustrative three-link self-correction sequence
code.code:
DRAFT CALL
Input: <source>original document</source>
Instruction: Draft a summary of the source.
Save output as: draft

REVIEW CALL
Input: <source>original document</source><draft>draft output</draft>
Instruction: List every claim in the draft that the source does not support.
Save output as: review

DECISION
If the review has no findings, keep the draft as the final output.
If the review has findings, continue to the revision call.

REVISION CALL
Input: <source>original document</source><draft>draft output</draft><review>review output</review>
Instruction: Revise the draft. Keep only claims supported by the source.
Save output as: final

LOG
Keep the draft, review, decision, and final output for inspection.

sections.title: Lay out long inputs deliberately, and do not grade the narrated reasoning
paragraphs: For long inputs, the order of the prompt matters. Anthropic's guide recommends placing long documents "near the top of your prompt, above your query, instructions, and examples," and notes that "queries at the end can improve response quality by up to 30 percent in tests, especially with complex, multidocument inputs." Google gives the same structural advice for Gemini: "supply all the context first" and place specific instructions or questions "at the very end of the prompt." Anthropic adds two refinements: wrap each document, with its source and content, in its own tags, and ask the model to quote the relevant passages before carrying out the task. The quotes become an intermediate artifact you can check against the source.

That last step matters because a model's written reasoning is itself generated text, not a transcript of its computation. Anthropic's research on reasoning models tested this by inserting hints about the answer into questions and checking whether the models' chains of thought admitted using them. On average across hint types, Claude 3.7 Sonnet mentioned the hint 25% of the time and DeepSeek R1 39% of the time. In experiments involving exploitable reward hacks, the models admitted using the hacks less than 2% of the time in most testing scenarios and sometimes supplied other rationales. The researchers conclude that "we can't always rely on what they tell us about their reasoning." Visible reasoning may help expose an obvious mistake, but acceptance decisions should rest on checks against sources, tests, and outputs rather than on whether an explanation sounds convincing.
sections.callout: Reasoning you can read is still output. Verify the answer against evidence; do not grade the explanation.

sections.title: Practice source: Harbor Room event agreement
paragraphs: The agreement below is an original fictional document created for this lesson. It is complete for the exercises that follow. Because every learner uses the same supplied source, the core practice can be completed offline without an AI account.

Treat each numbered clause as evidence. A claim passes an evidence check only when the cited clause supports it. If the document does not answer a question, report that the answer is not stated rather than filling the gap.
sections.callout: Fictional practice material. It is not a real contract and is not legal advice.

code.label: Complete fictional Harbor Room event agreement
code.code:
HARBOR ROOM EVENT AGREEMENT
Fictional practice document

1. PARTIES AND EVENT. Northstar Learning Cooperative, called the Organizer, books the Harbor Room from Seaview Community Center, called the Venue, for the Organizer's public workshop on October 18, 2026.

2. CAPACITY. Attendance must not exceed 120 people, including presenters and staff.

3. SCHEDULE. Organizer access begins at 8:00 a.m. Doors open to attendees at 9:00 a.m. The program begins at 9:30 a.m. and must end by 4:30 p.m. The room must be vacated by 5:30 p.m.

4. CATERING. The Venue will provide a vegetarian lunch and nonalcoholic drinks for the confirmed attendee count. The Organizer must provide the final attendee count and identified dietary restrictions by October 11, 2026.

5. DEPOSIT. The Organizer must pay a nonrefundable deposit of $2,000 when signing the agreement.

6. BALANCE. The remaining venue fee of $3,500 is due by October 4, 2026.

7. ORGANIZER CANCELLATION. If the Organizer cancels in writing on or before September 20, 2026, the Venue will refund any venue fee paid beyond the deposit. The deposit remains nonrefundable. If the Organizer cancels after September 20, 2026, amounts already paid are not refundable.

8. VENUE CANCELLATION. If the Venue cancels the event, it will refund all amounts the Organizer paid. The Venue is not responsible for the Organizer's travel, lodging, printing, or other indirect costs.

9. INCLUDED EQUIPMENT. The venue fee includes one projector, one projection screen, two handheld microphones, and standard room Wi-Fi. Additional equipment is not included.

10. ACCESSIBILITY REQUESTS. The Organizer must send requests for reserved accessible seating, live captioning, or other event-specific accessibility arrangements by September 27, 2026. The Venue will confirm in writing which requested arrangements it can provide.

11. PUBLICITY. The Organizer may use the Venue's name in factual event listings but may not state or imply that the Venue sponsors the workshop.

12. CHANGES. A change to this agreement is effective only if it is written and signed by both the Organizer and the Venue.

sections.title: Worked comparison: one call and an inspectable two-stage chain
paragraphs: The single-call version places the complete document first, separates it with tags, asks for supporting quotations, and puts the question last. Its supplied output is an illustration written for this lesson, not the result of a live model execution and not evidence of how any model will behave.

The two-stage version makes extraction independently inspectable. Its intentionally flawed intermediate output omits the on-or-before-September-20 Organizer cancellation case and says that the Venue must reimburse travel costs. Clause 7 supplies the omitted cancellation case, while clause 8 states that the Venue is not responsible for travel costs. The checks label the extraction incomplete, reject the unsupported reimbursement claim, and identify the controlling source evidence without speculating about why either error appeared.

The second stage receives both the original source and the intermediate extraction. It verifies each item, removes or corrects unsupported content, and produces the final summary. The checks evaluate quotations, clause references, dates, amounts, and scope. They do not request or grade private chain of thought.
sections.callout: Illustrative outputs show how to apply evidence checks. They do not prove actual model behavior.

If the Organizer cancels in writing by September 20, amounts paid beyond the deposit are refunded; after that date, amounts already paid are not refundable. SINGLE-CALL EVIDENCE CHECK
PASS: Every date and amount in the answer appears in a quoted clause.
PASS: The cancellation summary distinguishes Organizer cancellation from Venue cancellation.
PASS: The answer does not say that travel or other indirect costs will be reimbursed.
PASS: Each quotation is copied from the supplied document and carries the correct clause number.

TWO-STAGE CHAIN

STAGE 1 PROMPT: EXTRACT
<document>
Use the complete Harbor Room Event Agreement supplied in the preceding section. Clauses 1 through 12 are part of this stage's input.
</document>

Extract the payment terms, Organizer deadlines, and cancellation consequences. For each item, provide a short claim, a clause number, and an exact supporting quotation. Do not provide private reasoning. Return only the extraction table.

ILLUSTRATIVE STAGE 1 INTERMEDIATE OUTPUT
1. Claim: The $2,000 deposit is nonrefundable and due at signing.
   Clause: 5
   Quote: "The Organizer must pay a nonrefundable deposit of $2,000 when signing the agreement."
2. Claim: The $3,500 balance is due October 4, 2026.
   Clause: 6
   Quote: "The remaining venue fee of $3,500 is due by October 4, 2026."
3. Claim: Accessibility requests are due September 27, 2026.
   Clause: 10
   Quote: "The Organizer must send requests for reserved accessible seating, live captioning, or other event-specific accessibility arrangements by September 27, 2026."
4. Claim: The final attendee count and dietary restrictions are due October 11, 2026.
   Clause: 4
   Quote: "The Organizer must provide the final attendee count and identified dietary restrictions by October 11, 2026."
5. Claim: An Organizer cancellation after September 20 makes amounts already paid nonrefundable.
   Clause: 7
   Quote: "If the Organizer cancels after September 20, 2026, amounts already paid are not refundable."
6. Claim: If the Venue cancels, it refunds all payments and reimburses the Organizer's travel costs.
   Clause: 8
   Quote: "If the Venue cancels the event, it will refund all amounts the Organizer paid."

STAGE 1 EVIDENCE CHECK
INCOMPLETE: Items 1 through 5 have quotations that support their claims, but the extraction does not cover all requested cancellation consequences. It omits the clause 7 rule for an Organizer cancellation in writing on or before September 20, 2026, so the extraction must not receive a complete-coverage pass.
FAIL: Item 6 adds reimbursement of travel costs, but its quotation supports only a refund of amounts paid to the Venue. Clause 8 also says, "The Venue is not responsible for the Organizer's travel, lodging, printing, or other indirect costs." The unsupported travel-reimbursement claim must not pass to the final summary.

STAGE 2 PROMPT: VERIFY, CORRECT, AND SUMMARIZE
<document>
Use the complete Harbor Room Event Agreement supplied in the preceding section. Clauses 1 through 12 are part of this stage's input.
</document>
<extraction>
Insert the complete Stage 1 intermediate output here.
</extraction>

Check every extraction claim against the original document. Correct or remove any unsupported claim. Also check whether the extraction covers every requested payment term, Organizer deadline, and cancellation consequence; recover any omitted case from the original document before writing the summary. Then provide:
1. A verification list marking each extraction item SUPPORTED, PARTLY SUPPORTED, or UNSUPPORTED, with the controlling clause.
2. A coverage check that identifies and recovers any requested case omitted from the extraction.
3. A corrected summary of no more than 120 words.
Do not infer a reason for any error and do not provide private chain of thought.

Verification:
1. SUPPORTED, clause 5.
2. SUPPORTED, clause 6.
3. SUPPORTED, clause 10.
4. SUPPORTED, clause 4.
5. SUPPORTED, clause 7.

Supporting quote: "If the Organizer cancels in writing on or before September 20, 2026, the Venue will refund any venue fee paid beyond the deposit. The deposit remains nonrefundable."

Accessibility requests are due September 27, and the final attendee count and dietary restrictions are due October 11. If the Organizer cancels in writing on or before September 20, payments beyond the nonrefundable deposit are refunded; after September 20, amounts already paid are not refundable. If the Venue cancels, it refunds all amounts paid. It is not responsible for the Organizer's travel, lodging, printing, or other indirect costs.

PASS: All six supplied extraction items receive an explicit verification status.
FAIL THEN CORRECTED: The supplied extraction has incomplete cancellation coverage because it omits the on-or-before-September-20 case. Stage 2 recovers that case from clause 7 before producing the corrected summary.
PASS: The final summary corrects the unsupported travel-reimbursement claim using clause 8.

sections.title: Learner variation: answer a different operational question
paragraphs: Complete this variation without reusing the worked summary. It asks about a hypothetical event decision, included equipment, and publicity rather than asking for a general list of payments and deadlines. Use only the supplied Harbor Room agreement.
Write your answer before opening the key. For each sentence, record the clause that supports it. Mark a sentence for revision if its clause does not support the whole sentence.
The explained key shows both the expected conclusions and their limits. Specific feedback statements help distinguish a fully supported answer from common overclaims.

code.label: Offline learner task, explained answer key, and feedback
code.code:
LEARNER VARIATION

Scenario: The Organizer paid both the $2,000 deposit and the $3,500 balance early. On September 25, 2026, the Organizer considers cancelling. The team also wants a third handheld microphone and plans to advertise the Venue as a sponsor.

Task: Using only the Harbor Room Event Agreement, answer all three questions. Cite the controlling clause after each answer.

A. If the Organizer cancels in writing on September 25, how much of the $5,500 already paid does the agreement say is refundable?
B. Is a third handheld microphone included in the venue fee?
C. May the Organizer advertise that the Venue sponsors the workshop?

For each answer, copy one exact supporting quotation. If the agreement does not provide enough information, say so.

EVIDENCE CHECKS FOR THE LEARNER
1. Every conclusion has a clause number and an exact quotation.
2. The cancellation answer applies the rule for a date after September 20.
3. The equipment answer distinguishes the two included microphones from additional equipment.
4. The publicity answer distinguishes factual use of the Venue's name from a sponsorship claim.

EXPLAINED ANSWER KEY

A. None of the $5,500 already paid is refundable under the stated scenario. Clause 7 controls because September 25 is after September 20. Supporting quote: "If the Organizer cancels after September 20, 2026, amounts already paid are not refundable." The answer concerns only what this fictional agreement states. It should not add penalties or remedies that the document does not mention.

B. No. A third handheld microphone is not included. Clause 9 includes "two handheld microphones" and then states, "Additional equipment is not included." The document does not state whether a third microphone can be rented or what it would cost, so an answer should not invent those details.

C. No. Clause 11 permits the Organizer to use the Venue's name in factual event listings but says it "may not state or imply that the Venue sponsors the workshop." A correct answer may mention the permitted factual listing, but it must not convert that permission into a sponsorship claim.

SPECIFIC FEEDBACK

If you answered A with a full refund: Recheck the date. The full-refund rule in clause 8 applies when the Venue cancels, not when the Organizer cancels after September 20.

If you answered A with a $3,500 refund: You applied the on-or-before-September-20 rule. September 25 falls under the later-cancellation sentence, which says amounts already paid are not refundable.

If you answered B yes because microphones are listed: Compare the requested quantity with the included quantity. Clause 9 includes two, not three, and excludes additional equipment.

If you gave a rental price or said a third microphone is unavailable: The document supplies neither fact. Keep the supported conclusion that it is not included and state that rental availability and price are not specified.

If you answered C yes because the Venue's name may be used: Clause 11 permits factual listings but separately prohibits stating or implying sponsorship.

If all three answers match the key and each has the controlling quotation: Your conclusions are grounded in the supplied clauses and appropriately avoid filling information gaps.

activity.title: Re-architect one multi-step task two ways
instructions: Step 1: Work from the complete fictional Harbor Room Event Agreement in this module. No account, model, code, API, or outside document is required.

Step 2: Copy the worked single-call prompt structure, keeping the complete agreement first and the question last. Use the existing Learner Variation questions A, B, and C about September 25 cancellation, a third handheld microphone, and sponsorship publicity. Draft an illustrative answer yourself, cite the controlling clause after each answer, and copy one exact supporting quotation for each. Complete your answer before consulting the existing Explained Answer Key, then compare each answer with that key.

Step 3: Re-architect the same supplied A/B/C task as a two-stage chain. Stage 1 must extract claims, clause numbers, and exact quotations. Stage 2 must receive the original agreement and the Stage 1 output, verify every claim, and produce corrected final answers to A, B, and C.

Step 4: Write a separate pass or fail evidence check for each stage. Check whether every claim is supported by its quotation, whether the clause number is correct, and whether the final answer introduces any fact absent from the agreement.
Step 5: Compare the single-call result with the chain. Explain which errors the intermediate extraction would make easier to locate and what extra handoff the chain requires.

Optional actual model execution: You may run either prompt in a tool if permitted, but this is not required. Label the work as an actual run and record the tool or provider, model name or displayed model identifier, run date, exact prompt, raw output, and any settings the interface exposes. Do not claim that the supplied illustrative outputs came from that run, and do not submit private chain of thought.
evidence: A completed single-call prompt with the supplied agreement first, the existing Learner Variation questions A, B, and C last, quoted evidence, and learner-authored illustrative answers checked against the existing Explained Answer Key.
A completed two-stage chain showing the Stage 1 extraction, the Stage 2 verification and corrected answers to A, B, and C, and the original agreement available to both stages.
A per-stage evidence table with pass or fail results, cited clauses, and a correction for every failed claim.
A short architecture decision comparing what the chain makes inspectable with the cost of an additional handoff.

For a model documented as reasoning before it responds, give clear goals instead of scripted steps, and test whether the added reasoning cost improves results on the task.

Put long documents first and the question last, ground answers in quotes, and remember that a model's written reasoning is output, not a faithful record of how it decided.
Begin the check once learners can choose between built-in thinking, prompted reasoning, and a chain, and justify the choice by what each lets them inspect.

Introduce the Harbor Room agreement as the complete fictional evidence set for the remaining practice. Demonstrate that a claim passes only when a numbered clause supports the whole claim, and that missing information must be reported as unstated rather than inferred.

Walk through the document-first single-call prompt and then the two-stage chain. At Stage 1, stop on the unsupported travel-reimbursement claim, compare it with clause 8, mark the check failed, and show how Stage 2 corrects it without guessing why it appeared.

Ask learners to solve the cancellation, equipment, and publicity variation before reading the key. Emphasize that each conclusion needs an exact quotation and that unsupported rental terms, prices, remedies, or sponsorship permissions must be omitted.

instructorScript.reducedMotionAlternative: Present the reasoning-location comparison and the prompt-chain flow as static tables and a numbered list with focus-based highlighting instead of animated sequences.

questions.prompt: Which statement best describes the original chain-of-thought prompting result reported by Wei and colleagues in 2022?
choices: It proved that a model's written reasoning always reflects its internal computation
Worked examples showing intermediate reasoning steps improved sufficiently large models on arithmetic, commonsense, and symbolic reasoning tasks
Step-by-step prompts make every model more accurate regardless of its size
It removed the need to evaluate prompts on test cases
questions.explanation: The paper reports gains for sufficiently large models on those three task families. It did not establish that written reasoning is faithful, that the effect holds at every model size, or that evaluation is unnecessary.

questions.prompt: You are using a model whose provider documents it as reasoning internally. Which approach matches the guidance presented in this module?
choices: Always write a detailed hand-authored plan and demand a complete chain of thought
Remove all delimiters so instructions and evidence blend together
Give clear, direct instructions and a specific end goal instead of prescribing every reasoning step
Always add many worked examples before trying a direct prompt
questions.explanation: The module presents provider guidance to use simple, direct instructions and a specific end goal for a model documented as reasoning internally. It also recommends delimiters and trying a direct prompt before adding examples.

questions.prompt: When is an explicit prompt chain worth its extra calls?
choices: When you need to inspect intermediate outputs or enforce a specific pipeline structure
Whenever a task description is longer than one sentence
Only when no source documents are available
Never, because built-in thinking has made chaining obsolete
questions.explanation: A chain is useful when an intermediate result can be inspected, evaluated, or routed before the workflow continues. Task-description length alone is not the criterion.

questions.prompt: You are asking a question about a long report. Where should the question go according to the layout guidance in this module?
choices: At the beginning, before the report
Repeated at the start and end in different words
In a separate conversation that does not contain the report
After the report, at the end of the prompt
questions.explanation: The module recommends placing long source documents first and the specific question at the end so the context precedes the task.

questions.prompt: In the cited faithfulness experiments, how often did the tested models mention an inserted hint on average across hint types?
choices: Almost always, because reasoning models narrate every input they use
A minority of the time: 25% for Claude 3.7 Sonnet and 39% for DeepSeek R1
Never, because the models refused all hinted questions
Exactly half of the time for both models
questions.explanation: The module reports averages of 25% for Claude 3.7 Sonnet and 39% for DeepSeek R1. These results support treating visible reasoning as output that still requires verification.

questions.prompt: A review identifies unsupported claims in a draft. What must the revision call receive so it can verify the correction?
choices: Only the draft
Only the review
The original source, the draft, and the review
Only an instruction to make the writing more confident
questions.explanation: The revision call needs the original source as well as the draft and review. Without the source, it cannot independently verify whether the review findings or revised claims are supported.

questions.prompt: In the worked chain, Stage 1 says the Venue will reimburse the Organizer's travel costs if the Venue cancels. How should the evidence check classify that claim?
choices: Pass, because clause 8 requires a refund of all amounts paid
Pass, because travel is normally part of an event budget
Fail, because clause 8 says the Venue is not responsible for travel or other listed indirect costs
Unknown, because the model's private reasoning is unavailable
questions.explanation: Clause 8 expressly excludes responsibility for travel, lodging, printing, and other indirect costs. A refund of amounts paid to the Venue does not support travel reimbursement. The classification rests on the document, not on speculation about how the claim was produced.

questions.prompt: Why does the worked Stage 2 prompt include both the original agreement and the Stage 1 extraction?
choices: So the verifier can compare every extracted claim with the source and correct unsupported content
So the verifier can reveal the model's private chain of thought
So clause quotations no longer need to be checked
So the final answer may add reasonable details absent from the agreement
questions.explanation: The original agreement lets Stage 2 independently verify the extraction. The chain is designed to inspect claims and evidence, not to obtain private reasoning or authorize unsupported additions.

questions.prompt: In the learner variation, what does the agreement say about a third handheld microphone?
choices: It is included because microphones appear in clause 9
It is not included, and the agreement does not state its rental availability or price
It is prohibited at the event
It is included only if requested by September 27
questions.explanation: Clause 9 includes two handheld microphones and says additional equipment is not included. The agreement does not state whether another microphone can be rented or what it would cost, so those details must remain unstated.
